result.output:
===== 144496234 | 2026-08-23 | feat(client): OpenRouter app attribution headers
OpenRouter identifies calling apps on its public rankings through two
optional headers (HTTP-Referer, X-Title); there is no manual submission
path. Send them on OpenRouter routes only so Codewhale appears as
itself there:

- HTTP-Referer: https://codewhale.net
- X-Title: Codewhale

The headers identify the app, never the user. They are inserted before
the extra-header loop, so a user-configured header of the same name
still wins. The test pins both the OpenRouter-only scoping (checked
against several other providers) and the override precedence.

Entire-Checkpoint: 01M0RG547R5NFFNTRY4B62WSTN


===== e25e3b4b9 | 2026-08-23 | feat(client): OpenRouter app attribution headers
OpenRouter identifies calling apps on its public rankings through two
optional headers (HTTP-Referer, X-Title); there is no manual submission
path. Send them on OpenRouter routes only so Codewhale appears as
itself there:

- HTTP-Referer: https://codewhale.net
- X-Title: Codewhale

The headers identify the app, never the user. They are inserted before
the extra-header loop, so a user-configured header of the same name
still wins. The test pins both the OpenRouter-only scoping (checked
against several other providers) and the override precedence.

Entire-Checkpoint: 01M0RG547R5NFFNTRY4B62WSTN


===== ba19a15dc | 2026-08-20 | feat(tui): make the provider picker say where it looked for a key
A row that reads `missing key | key:not-set` tells a user nothing they
can act on. It does not say whether the durable slot was read and found
empty, read and skipped, or never consulted — so a home whose secret
store held a working DeepSeek key could show that row while a real turn
from the same home completed, and no layer on screen reported a source.

Every row now carries the resolution's source:

  Details pane gains `Credential: <place>` — "OPENROUTER_API_KEY",
  `secret store "deepseek"`, `[providers.x] api_key`, "xAI OAuth", a
  consented external CLI path, or "not found".

  The missing-key note gains the places that were probed, in precedence
  order, plus the command that fixes the first of them. Captured before
  and after, same fixture:

    before: missing OPENROUTER_API_KEY
    after:  missing OPENROUTER_API_KEY · checked env OPENROUTER_API_KEY,
            [providers.openrouter] api_key, secret store "openrouter"
            (not read: inactive provider, no api-key marker),
            ~/.codewhale/config.toml · fix: export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=<key>

Sources and fixes are labels only; a test asserts the note never carries
key material. Readiness labels, auth-status labels, and every `/provider`
subcommand are unchanged.

===== 068032b4f | 2026-08-03 | fix(config): resolve legacy dual-wire provider slugs to their own tables
The 19 red unit tests on the train tip were not env-key sensitivity and
not a PoisonError cascade; they were one root cause plus its fallout.

Root cause: d53f4f998 ("dialect is wire config, not catalog rows") added
the legacy dual-wire slugs to the vendor primaries' ProviderKind alias
lists, so ApiProvider::parse collapsed "deepseek-anthropic" onto Deepseek
and "minimax-anthropic" onto Minimax. Every route-scoped lookup keyed off
api_provider() — credentials, base_url, model — then read the primary's
empty table and orphaned the [providers.deepseek-anthropic] /
[providers.minimax-anthropic] table the config actually selects. Twelve
client tests panicked with "DeepSeek/MiniMax API key not found" despite
fixture keys sitting in the legacy table, and the retired-alias effort
inference lost the provider-scoped model id (config::tests::
retired_deepseek_aliases_keep_mode_intent_unless_effort_is_explicit).
Real pre-0.9.4 configs of that shape hit the same "API key not found" at
runtime, so fixture edits or skips would have papered over a regression.

Fix: ApiProvider::parse resolves the legacy dual-wire spellings to their
exact variants (DeepseekAnthropic / MinimaxAnthropic, with the pre-d53
alias spellings) before delegating to ProviderKind::parse. Catalog

# CodeWhale Inference diligence — 19 August 2026

Evidence labels used below: **verified** means a primary source was checked on 19 August 2026; **catalog** means a live provider catalog claim, not a contractual guarantee; **empirical** means an observed public trace or dataset; **assumption** means a deliberately visible scenario input; **negotiation** means no public entitlement exists. Prices are per one million tokens unless stated otherwise. This is product and technical diligence, not legal or tax advice.

## 1. Executive recommendation

**Build as a small experiment, not as a general-availability inference business.** Ship an invite-only, prepaid DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 pilot behind CodeWhale keys. Keep V4 Pro 0813 BYOK-only or disabled until Shannon Labs has a written wholesale agreement, an exact-revision attestation, and request-level settlement data.

The opportunity is real but narrower than the original thesis:

- DeepSeek's direct API has a simple 2× peak multiplier. A fixed CodeWhale rate below direct peak is mathematically possible whenever traffic is not 100% peak, but a direct-only business loses money at 100% peak unless retail is at least the peak rate.
- Flash has multiple cataloged exact-0731 hosts at fixed prices below DeepSeek peak. That can hedge the peak window, subject to revision, cache, privacy, capacity, and resale verification.
- Pro does not yet have a dependable spread. Fireworks' exact 0813 public rate equals DeepSeek peak in each category, while OpenRouter's aggregate 0813 quote leaves only a thin spread that its 5.5% credit-purchase fee can consume. Vercel lists a pinned `deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro-0813` ID in its live `/v1/models` feed, but its indexed provider pages still describe the April 0423 model and old promotional prices. That is not launch-grade evidence.
- CodeWhale's shipped central telemetry cannot produce per-user token or cost percentiles. Local runtime records already distinguish fresh input, cache reads, cache writes, output, reasoning, model, provider, and cost provenance, but [central telemetry](../TELEMETRY.md) intentionally collects neither model IDs nor request-level token ledgers. Subscription allowances would therefore be guesswork today.
- Gateway resale is not just an implementation question. DeepSeek's current Open Platform terms expressly contemplate applications for external end users, but Vercel's general license says internal business use while its AI Gateway section expressly contemplates customer Applications and End Users. Counsel and written provider confirmation should resolve that drafting tension before paid resale.

Pilot exit gates: at least 10,000 paid requests and 200 trajectories; exact revision returned and stored on 100% of requests; request cost reconciles to upstream statements within 0.5%; no silent cross-model fallback; P95 margin after payment, support, bad debt, and credits remains positive; and a provider or counsel confirms downstream resale in writing. Do not make a public price promise before those gates.

## 2. Current DeepSeek pricing

### Models and behavior

DeepSeek's [live USD pricing page](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/pricing/), [live RMB pricing page](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/zh-cn/quick_start/pricing/), and [change log](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/updates/) identify the currently relevant coding/agent models:

| Public selection | API `model` | Actual current revision | Release | Context / max output | Modality | Reasoning and tools |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek V4 Flash | `deepseek-v4-flash` | `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731` | 2026-07-31 | 1M / 384K | text in, text out | thinking and non-thinking; thinking is default; `low`, `high`, `max`; tools, JSON, Responses, Anthropic; FIM only non-thinking |
| DeepSeek V4 Pro | `deepseek-v4-pro` | `DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813` | 2026-08-13 | 1M / 384K | text in, text out | same surface; Pro GA added the 0813 post-training revision |

Neither official API model supports image, audio, or video input. The Flash [official model card](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731) describes a 304B-parameter release checkpoint; Pro is 1.6T total / 49B active. The undated API IDs are aliases, so CodeWhale must store both the requested ID and the response's actual revision and must pause a route if the latter changes.

Reasoning tokens are reported inside `completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens` in the [chat-completion schema](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/api/create-chat-completion/); they are a subset of completion/output tokens, not an additional billable category. The ledger should expose them but must not double-charge them. DeepSeek's [thinking guide](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/thinking_mode/) also requires preserving reasoning state across tool calls according to the selected API format.

### Current variable list pricing

| Model | Currency/window | Cache-hit input | Fresh/cache-miss input | Output, including reasoning |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Flash 0731 | USD off-peak | $0.007 | $0.22 | $0.66 |
| Flash 0731 | USD peak | $0.014 | $0.44 | $1.32 |
| Pro 0813 | USD off-peak | $0.022 | $0.66 | $1.98 |
| Pro 0813 | USD peak | $0.044 | $1.32 | $3.96 |
| Flash 0731 | CNY off-peak | ¥0.05 | ¥1.50 | ¥4.50 |
| Flash 0731 | CNY peak | ¥0.10 | ¥3.00 | ¥9.00 |
| Pro 0813 | CNY off-peak | ¥0.15 | ¥4.50 | ¥13.50 |
| Pro 0813 | CNY peak | ¥0.30 | ¥9.00 | ¥27.00 |

Peak is **09:00–12:00 and 14:00–18:00 Beijing time (UTC+8)**, equivalently **01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC**. All other time is off-peak. This is a rate window, not a promotion.

The USD and RMB cards are separate commercial price lists, not mechanical FX conversions. At the 19 August indicative market quote of roughly ¥6.73 per dollar (the official daily reference should be pulled from [CFETS](https://www.chinamoney.org.cn/english/bmkrrtrrt/) at settlement), Flash off-peak fresh input at ¥1.50 is about $0.223, close to the USD card, while other cells differ slightly. CodeWhale should price each billing entity from its lawful local supply and settlement costs, not use geography to conceal a markup.

### Cache rules

DeepSeek's [KV-cache documentation](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/kv_cache/) says caching is automatic and best effort. Complete repeated prefixes are detected at request boundaries and `prompt_cache_hit_tokens` / `prompt_cache_miss_tokens` are returned. Cache entries usually survive hours to days, can take seconds to construct, and are not guaranteed. There is no published cache-write fee and no independent cache-write usage field; CodeWhale may measure tokens admitted to its own prefix plan, but upstream billable cache write is zero/unknown rather than invented. `user_id` isolates KV cache and scheduling under one upstream account; it must be opaque and contain no personal data. Current account concurrency is 2,500 Flash and 500 Pro, with 429 beyond those limits ([rate-limit documentation](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/rate_limit)).

### Pricing taxonomy

- **Permanent/list pricing:** the current peak and off-peak cards above, effective 16 August 2026 16:00 UTC for the new tariff. “Permanent” here means current list, not immutable; DeepSeek reserves the right to change it.
- **Variable pricing:** the 2× windows above.
- **Historical/promotion:** the April V4 preview card showed Flash $0.0028 cached / $0.14 fresh / $0.28 output and Pro $0.003625 / $0.435 / $0.87. Those are not today's rates. Some gateways still display them as a 75%-off Pro promotion. Do not use them for forward economics.
- **Temporary promotions now:** none was found on DeepSeek's current official pricing or change-log pages. Alibaba explicitly says console promotions are excluded from its public list card; those offers must not fund CodeWhale's base case.
- **Announced future changes:** none beyond the tariff already effective on 16 August was found in current official sources.
- **Negotiated pricing:** no public DeepSeek volume discount was found. Any discount in this report is a proposed negotiation, not an entitlement.

The same `https://api.deepseek.com` base URL is shown in English and Chinese documentation. Public documentation does not promise distinct international versus mainland inference residency, retention, or SLA. Currency/account availability and legal entity differ; obtain a DPA and residency statement rather than inferring them from localized documentation.

## 3. Vercel pricing

Vercel AI Gateway currently advertises zero token markup, prepaid credits by default, BYOK with no gateway token fee, and enterprise consolidated invoicing ([pricing](https://vercel.com/docs/ai-gateway/pricing), [product page](https://vercel.com/ai-gateway)). Payment-processing fees and separately metered features can still apply. ### Routing, cost, and controls

The current [model API documentation](https://vercel.com/ai-gateway/models/deepseek-v4-pro/api) defines:

- `only`: hard provider allowlist; failure if none can serve.
- `order`: preferred order; unlisted providers remain fallbacks.
- `sort: cost | ttft | tps`: provider ordering. `cost` is catalog/input-price oriented and is not a trajectory/cache-loss optimizer.
- `zeroDataRetention`: filters to eligible endpoints.

Gateway does same-model provider failover. Do not pass a multi-model fallback list: that would violate CodeWhale's identity promise. Pinning a provider is possible with a one-element `only`; provider order is possible with `order` plus `only` to prevent unlisted fallback.

Vercel's [cost-accounting exercise](https://vercel.com/academy/ai-gateway/ai-gateway-pricing) documents `providerMetadata.gateway.cost` as the actual request charge and says it should reconcile with the dashboard. `routing.finalProvider` is the provider that completed the request and is suitable for disclosure. `routing.resolvedProvider` appears in observed payloads/errors but has no stable public semantic contract; do not treat it as the actual server. Fields observed in raw metadata such as `gateway.inferenceCost`, `gateway.gatewayCost`, `marketCost`, or input/output inference splits are not sufficiently documented to be accounting authority. Store the raw receipt, use `gateway.cost` when present, calculate a timestamped estimate independently, and reconcile asynchronously.

Streaming is supported across AI SDK, Chat Completions, Responses, Messages, and OpenResponses. Gateway dashboards report request volume, spend, token counts, TTFT, provider, and model. Rate limits are plan/account dependent rather than a universal public number. Per-key budgets exist but a request can cross the threshold before the next request is rejected; CodeWhale still needs preauthorization and balance reservation. ZDR is per-provider; team-wide ZDR is separately metered on some plans, and BYOK inherits the upstream key's policy. Never turn a Gateway ZDR checkbox into a claim about a route that did not qualify.

## 5. Fixed-price opportunity

Let `p` be the share of requests' billable tokens occurring in DeepSeek peak windows. Direct blended COGS for a category is `off × (1 + p)` because peak is 2× off. The strict interval is:

`off × (1 + p) < fixed retail < peak`.

| Off/peak traffic | Peak share `p` | Flash lower bounds: cached / fresh / output | Pro lower bounds: cached / fresh / output |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 100/0 | 0% | $0.007 / $0.220 / $0.660 | $0.022 / $0.660 / $1.980 |
| 80/20 | 20% | $0.0084 / $0.264 / $0.792 | $0.0264 / $0.792 / $2.376 |
| 70/30 | 30% | $0.0091 / $0.286 / $0.858 | $0.0286 / $0.858 / $2.574 |
| 50/50 | 50% | $0.0105 / $0.330 / $0.990 | $0.0330 / $0.990 / $2.970 |
| 30/70 | 70% | $0.0119 / $0.374 / $1.122 | $0.0374 / $1.122 / $3.366 |
| 0/100 | 100% | $0.014 / $0.440 / $1.320 | $0.044 / $1.320 / $3.960 |

The upper bounds are always Flash `$0.014 / $0.44 / $1.32` and Pro `$0.044 / $1.32 / $3.96`. At 100% peak the interval is empty. With a 5% reserve for gateway/payment/support/reconciliation, multiply the lower bounds by 1.05; at 70% peak, Pro's remaining interval is only `$0.03927–0.044 / $1.1781–1.32 / $3.5343–3.96`.

For exact Flash-0731, Vercel's Runware catalog row would create wholesale-to-DeepSeek-peak intervals of `$0.01–0.014 cached`, `$0.08–0.44 fresh`, and `$0.15–1.32 output` before overhead. This is economically attractive but not yet contractually bankable. For exact Pro-0813, Fireworks equals direct peak; no strict interval exists. OpenRouter's aggregate quote is about 10% under peak, but its credit fee and endpoint mix leave an inadequate safety margin.

Therefore: a fixed, below-peak Flash offer is plausible after supplier qualification. A below-peak Pro promise is not presently sustainable. Autonomous workload geography is irrelevant; measure each ledger event's UTC timestamp. Offer “run at lowest-cost window” only for explicitly deferrable jobs, never interactive inference.

## 6. Agentic workload evidence

No conversational unit is used here. The evidence is request- and trajectory-based.

- A 2026 study of eight models, four independent runs, and 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks reports **4.17M average total tokens per agentic task**, input/output ratio about **153.85**, a roughly **7M-token difference** between the cheapest and most expensive task means, and up to **30×** same-task run variation in the broader analysis. Input dominates; in its Claude phase analysis, cache-read input dominates both raw tokens and dollars despite output being about 80× dearer per token ([paper/project](https://longjubai.github.io/agent_token_consumption/), [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22750)). This is benchmark evidence, not a user/month distribution.
- Microsoft's Orchard dataset reports 107,185 generated software-engineering trajectories with median estimated 19,085 tokens, mean 20,823, P95 39,267, max 100,997. These are training trajectories with estimated tokens and are much shorter than frontier OpenHands SWE-bench runs; they demonstrate harness/model dependence, not a retail baseline ([dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/microsoft/Orchard)).
- The public Ninja SWE Agent dataset contains 1,009 Claude Sonnet 4 rollouts. Its cost P50/P75/P90/P95/P99 is approximately $0.083/$0.127/$0.188/$0.223/$0.286 and output-token P50/P75/P90/P95/P99 is 6,137/9,016/12,729/15,127/19,274. However, only 123 rows have nonzero input-token fields and 874 have nonzero cost, so input distributions are not reliable and are excluded. This is an example of why schema completeness must gate analysis ([dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/unconst/ninja-swe-agent)).
- OpenHands' current public index reports benchmark-level average dollars and runtimes by model, not separable cache/fresh token ledgers. It is useful for cross-model cost comparison, not CodeWhale pricing ([index](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenHands/openhands-index)).
- A [reported autonomous fleet example](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/openclaw-creator-burns-through-1-3-million-in-openai-api-tokens-in-a-single-month) reached 603B tokens over 7.6M requests and roughly 100 coding agents in 30 days—about 79K raw tokens per upstream request and 6.03B tokens per agent-month if evenly divided. It is a secondary report of a dashboard screenshot and an extreme organizational workload, not a consumer estimate, but it confirms the heavy tail and the need for monetary circuit breakers.

Evidence does not support one “small/medium/large” numeric truth. Sections 9 and 17 therefore keep empirical distributions separate from transparent stress envelopes.

## 7. Inference-ledger model

One immutable ledger row per upstream attempt:

```text
request_id, attempt_id, timestamp_utc
customer_id, api_key_id, task_id, trajectory_id
requested_product, requested_revision
actual_model, actual_revision, provider, supply_product_id
fresh_input_tokens, cache_read_tokens, cache_write_tokens
output_tokens, reasoning_tokens_subset
request_latency_ms, ttft_ms, generation_ms
price_window, provider_price_version_id
upstream_reported_cost, calculated_upstream_cost, reconciled_cost
retail_price_version_id, retail_charge, gross_profit
status, retry_of, fallback_from, fallback_reason
usage_source, cost_source, raw_receipt_hash
```

For a provider with separate prices:

`COGS = fresh×Pf + cache_read×Pr + cache_write×Pw + output×Po + request_fees + gateway_fees`.

`reasoning_tokens ≤ output_tokens`; it is informational unless the provider explicitly prices it separately. DeepSeek currently does not. Raw processed volume is `fresh + cache_read + cache_write + output`; billable economic volume is the dollar expression, not a token sum.

Every price row is effective-dated with currency, timezone, peak predicate, source URL/hash, tax treatment, and whether it is list, promotion, or contract. Authorize with a conservative maximum estimate, reserve balance atomically, settle on the final receipt, and release the remainder. Never wait for a monthly provider invoice to infer per-request margin.

Vercel `gateway.cost` or another documented provider receipt becomes `upstream_reported_cost`; the independent rate calculation becomes `calculated_upstream_cost`. A mismatch opens reconciliation and can quarantine the supply product. Unknown usage never becomes zero cost.

## 8. Cache economics

Define cache rate precisely as **cache-read share of input tokens**:

`h = cache_read / (fresh_input + cache_read)`.

For 100M input tokens, excluding output, DeepSeek off-peak cost is:

| `h` | Flash input COGS | Pro input COGS |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0% | $22.000 | $66.000 |
| 25% | $16.675 | $50.050 |
| 50% | $11.350 | $34.100 |
| 75% | $6.025 | $18.150 |
| 90% | $2.830 | $8.580 |
| 95% | $1.765 | $5.390 |
| 98% | $1.126 | $3.476 |

Peak doubles those values. Output must then be added independently. “95% cached” is therefore meaningful only over input tokens, not requests, and says nothing about output/reasoning.

Provider caches are not portable. Moving a trajectory can turn expected cache reads into fresh input, can change the cache discount, and can lose latency benefits. Vercel and OpenRouter routing do not create a cross-provider shared KV cache. DeepSeek cache is user-isolated, automatic, and hours-to-days best effort; Fireworks and other hosts publish different or incomplete semantics.

Use trajectory stickiness:

```text
expected_switch_cost =
  current_request_COGS(candidate)
  + P(cache_miss_after_switch) × reusable_prefix_tokens
    × (candidate_fresh_rate - incumbent_cache_rate)
  + latency_penalty_usd
  + failure_probability × retry_cost
  + privacy_or_policy_penalty
```

Switch only when candidate savings over a horizon exceed cache-loss cost plus a safety margin, or when health/privacy makes the incumbent ineligible. Stickiness key should include customer isolation and actual model revision. Preserve prefix stability: invariant constitution/system tools first, stable repository snapshot next, append-only trajectory/tool results last. Do not reorder or inject provider-specific text ahead of the reusable prefix.

##### FLASH-LOCAL-VERIFICATION #####
# Flash local verification — 2026-08-20

Evidence level: **local**. This is not deployed, production-accepted, a provider
cache canary, or permission to sell downstream inference.

## Result

The Flash Worker is runnable as a local HTTP service and its implemented product
contract matches the reviewed card.

- `GET /healthz` returned `200` with `codewhale-inference`.
- `GET /v1/models` exposed only Flash 0731 as `pilot`, with the fixed
  `$0.007 / $0.220 / $0.660` per-million cached-input, fresh-input, and output
  card. Pro 0813 remained `byok_only`.
- An unauthenticated balance read returned `401 invalid_api_key`.
- A Pro 0813 completion returned `503 model_not_enabled`.
- A Flash request whose declared maximum cost could not cover its conservative
  reservation returned `400 max_cost_too_low` before an upstream request.
- The protected activation path created the same purchase id idempotently.
- At its start time, `GET /v1/balance` reported week 1 active with a `$3.00`
  allowance and a `60,000,000` input-token ceiling.
- No real provider credential or request was used.

The isolated server used loopback port `8791` and inspector port `9291`.
It was stopped after the smoke. Its temporary Durable Object state, response
files, and fake environment file were removed, and no matching process remained.

## Automated gates

`npm run check && npm run deploy:dry-run` passed:

- 3 test files, 16 tests, all passing.
- Type generation and TypeScript checking passed.
- Dry-run bundle: 61.81 KiB, 13.83 KiB gzip.

## Gates that remain open

- Founder approval for the managed-supply exception to the BYOK posture.
- Written downstream resale and data-term approval from OpenRouter and
  DeepInfra.
- A qualifying cache canary with matching provider billing evidence.
- Supported Stripe secret custody and a real payment webhook.
- Production ledger projection, reconciliation, abuse controls, privacy/legal
  review, migration, deployment, and first live charge.

These are fail-closed launch gates, not defects hidden by the local result.

#section("CodeWhale")

#entry(
  "CodeWhale",
  "Creator and sole maintainer, Shannon Labs",
  "Jan 2026 – present",
)

Open-source coding agent for the terminal, written in Rust. Model, interface, and compute stay
decoupled, so any hosted or local model can serve a session.

- Grew from a terminal experiment to *40.8k stars, 3.5k forks, and 180+ contributors* in seven
  months. MIT licensed.
- Ships the routing surface directly: one agent loop across many providers, where nominally
  identical model IDs behave differently depending on who serves them.
- Basis of an ongoing public argument that harness design, not model choice alone, accounts for a
  large share of measured agent performance.

#section("Research")

#entry(
  "LLM evaluation and routing methodology",
  "Arcee AI",
  "June – Aug 2026",
)

Authored the evaluation and routing contract for a multi-provider agent platform.

- Separated three evaluation lanes — fixed-model harness comparison, plan-realistic product, and
  routing ablation — so routing gains cannot be confounded with harness effects or model mix.
- Specified routing ablations against fixed-fallback, validation-selected-fixed, and a post-hoc
  oracle upper bound, with the oracle held as a research ceiling and never a reportable score.
- Made provider identity first-class: nominally identical model IDs are recorded as provider,
  effective model, and revision, because hosts serve and route them differently.
- Addressed benchmark validity directly — rolling held-out suites against contamination, audited
  samples of passes and failures, and cost, tokens, and latency on the same attempts as quality.

#v(0.34em)

- *Shannon Control Unit* (2025) — a closed-loop PI controller holds the MDL information ratio at a
  target during training, in place of a fixed penalty tuned ahead of the run. *6–12% bits-per-token
  improvement* over tuned baselines; provisional patent filed Sept 2025.
- Keynote and invited talks in China on harness engineering — *GTLC*, *Hangzhou*, and *Ningxia*
  (2026); interviewed by *InfoQ*.

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content - tables, code, diagrams - gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

The two densest seams weren't in the code — they were in `docs/research/CODEWHALE_INFERENCE_DILIGENCE_2026-08-19.md` and the session where you pulled the live `/endpoints` feed for `deepseek-v4-flash-0731` and priced 30 hosts against it.

**The five things worth building an interview around:**

1. **You made OpenRouter the front door.** Commit `3d65cda02` rewrote the README lede, the guide, the website hero, and the localized dictionaries around "install Codewhale, add one OpenRouter key." That's the buy decision they want app developers to make, and you can explain why you made it.
2. **The reasoning-effort dialect matrix.** `apply_reasoning_effort` in `client.rs` is a ~40-arm match because every direct provider needs a different JSON shape. OpenRouter is the one arm where the user's choice passes through unmodified. That's a real product advantage they don't market.
3. **Thirty endpoints, one slug.** The cheapest was $0.065/M at fp4/262K; the *most expensive* was also fp4 with a truncated window. Price encodes neither quality nor context.
4. **Cost-optimal routing made the bill go up.** `sort: "cost"` reshuffles endpoints mid-trajectory and burns the prefix cache. Your own Terminal-Bench leg was 98.9% cache reads. This is the most research-shaped insight you have and it's a live open problem at their scale.
5. **Fail-closed identity.** The Worker pins `provider:{only, order, allow_fallbacks, require_parameters, quantizations}`, reads `openrouter_metadata.endpoints.available[].selected` back for a receipt, and refuses delivery if the returned `model` ≠ the pinned slug.

content.text:
Root cause confirmed — the live process carries it on its command line:

```
harbor run ... --n-concurrent 4 ...   (PID 54918, started 7:02PM)
```

**What happened.** `scripts/run-campaign-tb21-20260811.sh` sets `N_CONCURRENT="${CAMPAIGN_N_CONCURRENT:-4}"` — the runner's own default is 4. The 08-23 wrapper `launch-campaign.sh` pins it to 2, and that's why the three older legs are clean. The 0.9.11 leg was launched without going through that wrapper, so it inherited the runner default. No code was ever edited to cause this; the pin was just bypassed.

**Which legs are affected** (measured from trial intervals, not from config):

| Leg | Observed concurrency |
|---|---|
| cw097 high · pi0842 high · cw097 max2 | 2 throughout — clean |
| **cw0911 max** | ramps 1→2, then **3–6, settling at 4** |
| cw097 max (abandoned first max leg) | 3–4 — already superseded by max2 |

**Your "around 30" is close.** The exact shape:

- Trials 1–16 run at c ≤ 2. **All sixteen pass.**
- Trial 17 — `cancel-async-tasks`, 01:15:20 UTC, c=2 — is the **first failure**.
- At **01:28:31 UTC** six trials start in the same second (trials 19–24). That's the widening. It settles at c=4 from trial 38 onward and stays there for the rest of the leg.

One correction worth having straight: the first failure lands one burst *before* the widening, at c=2 — so it isn't itself a contention casualty. The pattern that the widening explains is what comes after it.

**The effect size, and why it matters:**

```
c<=2 :  23 trials · pass 82.6% · timeouts  1/23  (4.3%)
c>=3 :  59 trials · pass 74.6% · timeouts 13/59  (22.0%)
                                 Fisher exact two-sided p = 0.099
```

That 8-point pass gap is the same magnitude as the "regression" I reported an hour ago (0.9.11 77.2% vs 0.9.7 81.0%). So the apparent regression is plausibly scheduling contention, not the 0.9.11 build. Good catch.

**No hack needed** — `CAMPAIGN_N_CONCURRENT=2` is already what the wrapper exports. Re-running correctly means launching through `launch-campaign.sh`, not editing anything.

Two things I need from you before I spend the hours, since the job is still live and this is real API money:

questions.question: What scope should the c=2 re-run cover?

options.label: Full 89 at c=2, new job dir (Recommended)
options.description: ~14h, matches the campaign's own rule that a material config defect forces a rerun under a newly frozen configuration. Directly comparable to the completed cw097 max2 leg, which is also a full 89 at c=2. Leaves the contaminated run in place as evidence of the contention effect.
options.preview:
CAMPAIGN_N_CONCURRENT=2 \
  CAMPAIGN_JOB_SUFFIX=-0911c2 \
  ./launch-campaign.sh

-> cw0911-96d13a0c-flash-max-n1-20260823-0911c2
   89 trials, c=2, ~14h
   original -0911 job untouched

options.label: Only the 59 trials that ran at c>=3
options.description: ~9.5h. Cheaper and faster, but the resulting leg is stitched from two scheduling regimes, so it's weaker evidence than a clean full run.
options.preview:
harbor run ... --n-concurrent 2 \
  --task adaptive-rejection-sampler \
  --task bn-fit-modify ... (59 tasks)

-> 59 re-run at c=2
 + 23 original at c=2
 = 82 stitched

options.label: Don't re-run — report the confound
options.description: Zero cost. Use the c<=2 subset (n=23, 82.6%) and state that the 0.9.11 leg is not comparable to the c=2 legs. Honest, but n=23 is very thin.
options.preview:
No new trials.

Brief says:
  0.9.11 leg measured at c=4,
  not comparable to the c=2 legs.
  Clean subset n=23, 82.6%.

questions.question: The 0.9.11 job is still running (PID 54918, 3 pending / 4 in flight). What should I do with it?

options.label: Let it finish first (Recommended)
options.description: Roughly 30-60 min at its current rate. Completes the contaminated leg so the contention comparison has a full 89-trial denominator, then I launch the clean run.

wait for PID 54918 to exit

then launch c=2 run

options.description: Starts the clean run ~45 min sooner. The last 7 trials of the contaminated leg are lost, which slightly weakens the c>=3 sample.

Running: 2 in flight, 65 pending, `--n-concurrent 2` confirmed on the wire.

**Root cause — and it's better than "someone forgot."** The original launch line *did* pin it:

```
tmux ... -s tb21-0911-full  cd … && export CAMPAIGN_ID=20260823 CAMPAIGN_N_ATTEMPTS=1 \
    CAMPAIGN_N_CONCURRENT=2 … && bash scripts/run-campaign-tb21-20260811.sh codewhale
```

Those `export`s never reached the script — the tmux command was passed as unquoted argv rather than a single shell command — so `N_CONCURRENT="${CAMPAIGN_N_CONCURRENT:-4}"` in `run-campaign-tb21-20260811.sh` fell through to its default of **4**. The live process carried `--n-concurrent 4` on its command line, and the trial-interval measurement independently showed 3–6 in flight. Two independent confirmations, and the intent was 2 all along. It's a quoting bug in one launch line, not a config decision.

**The timeline, precisely.** Trials 1–16 all pass at c ≤ 2. Trial 17 — `cancel-async-tasks`, 01:15:20 UTC — is the first failure, and it's still at c=2. At **01:28:31 UTC** six trials start in the same second (trials 19–24); that's the widening, settling at c=4 from trial 38 on. So your "around 30" was right about where things go wrong, though the very first failure lands one burst before the widening rather than because of it.

**What I did:**

- Killed PID 54918. Checked the three lingering Docker containers first — they belong to `memory-footprint-20260824`, not this job, so I left them.
- Recomputed the split with intervals bounded at kill time rather than left open, which shifted it slightly from my earlier estimate: **22 clean at c ≤ 2**, **61 contaminated at c ≥ 3**, **6 never scored**. Re-run set is 61 + 6 = **67**, which reconstitutes a full 89-task leg when combined with the 22 clean ones.
- Verified the resolved JobConfig before launching: `n_concurrent_trials = 2`, 67 tasks, same bundle (`campaign-0911-96d13a0b`), model, endpoint, retry policy, effort.
- Launched as `cw0911-96d13a0c-flash-max-n1-20260823-0911c2` in tmux session `tb21-0911c2` on the same `cwbench20260823` socket. **The contaminated `-0911` job dir is intact** — it's the evidence for the contention effect.

No repo code was edited. The whole thing is env vars plus 67 `--include-task-name` flags. Two files added alongside the existing campaign launchers: `launch-0911c2.sh` and `0911c2-tasks.txt`.

content.text:
Done, essentially — 60 of 67 scored (7 errored out on infrastructure, 1 still in flight). Here's the whole thing, and it does not say what the early samples suggested.

**The concurrency effect, paired on 55 tasks:**

```
original c>=3 ... 42 pass   76.4%   timeouts 14 (25%)
re-run   c=2 .... 43 pass   78.2%   timeouts  9 (16%)

fail -> pass (6): compile-compcert, raman-fitting, regex-chess,
                  rstan-to-pystan, torch-pipeline-parallelism, tune-mjcf
pass -> fail (5): bn-fit-modify, build-cython-ext, largest-eigenval,
                  polyglot-rust-c, protein-assembly
McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.00
```

Six flips one way, five the other. **Net +1 task out of 55. p = 1.00.** There is no measurable concurrency effect on pass rate.

I have to walk back what I told you at 01:20. At 4:1 discordant I said the signal was "firming up" — it wasn't; it was a small sample that regressed to nothing as the remaining 34 tasks landed. The tasks that flipped toward pass were the long ones, which is the shape I predicted, but an almost equal number flipped the other way, which is just run-to-run noise at n=1. I should have held the line I took at the start of the night — five discordant pairs prove nothing — instead of reading the trend.

Timeouts did drop, 25% → 16%. That's the one real effect, and it's the mechanism you'd expect. It just didn't convert into pass rate.

**The repaired 0.9.11 leg vs 0.9.7, paired on 79 tasks:**

```
0.9.11 (repaired) ... 63/79 = 79.7%
0.9.7  (complete) ... 64/79 = 81.0%
only 0.9.11 wins: 7   ·   only 0.9.7 wins: 8
McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.00
```

So the answer to the original question is: **0.9.11 and 0.9.7 are indistinguishable.** The repaired leg is 79.3% against 0.9.7's 80.2%. The "3-point regression" I reported before the re-run was 76.8% vs 81.0% — the re-run closed about half of that gap and the rest was never significant to begin with. No regression, and no evidence the contamination mattered much either.

Net result of the whole exercise: you spent eight hours of compute to convert a soft false alarm into a clean null. That is a real outcome — the release gate says nothing is wrong — but it's worth being clear that the concurrency fix didn't rescue a finding, it dissolved one.

For the interview, this strengthens rather than weakens the story. You now have two independent null results from the same campaign at p = 1.00, and the honest version — *single-attempt runs on an 89-task suite cannot resolve differences of the size people argue about, and I have the paired data to prove it* — is a better answer than any score would have been.

content.text:
It finished at 07:53 and I hadn't checked since — that's the whole of "what happened." All six landed:

```
build-pmars ......... PASS
dna-insert .......... PASS
hf-model-inference .. PASS
write-compressor .... PASS
sanitize-git-repo ... FAIL
query-optimize ...... FAIL (agent timeout — now scored 0 instead of vanishing)
                      4 pass / 6
```

Four of the five apt casualties passed once they got a working `apt-get`. That confirms they were infra, not capability — they'd have been silently dropped from the denominator otherwise.

**The 0.9.11 leg is now complete: 89 of 89 scored, 70 pass, 78.7%.** Assembled from 22 original clean trials at c=2, 61 from the c=2 re-run, and 6 from the c=1 fair-shot pass.

**Final head-to-head, paired on 86 tasks:**

```
0.9.11 (repaired) ... 68/86 = 79.1%
0.9.7  (max2) ....... 69/86 = 80.2%

only 0.9.11 wins: 7   crack-7z-hash, db-wal-recovery, model-extraction-relu-logits,
                      raman-fitting, regex-chess, torch-pipeline-parallelism, video-processing
only 0.9.7  wins: 8   bn-fit-modify, build-cython-ext, cancel-async-tasks, install-windows-3.11,
                      largest-eigenval, polyglot-rust-c, protein-assembly, qemu-startup
McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.00
```

Seven against eight. **One task apart on 86, p = 1.00.** 0.9.11 and 0.9.7 are indistinguishable.

Where the whole night landed: the "3-point regression" I reported to you at the start was 76.8% vs 81.0%. Roughly half of that gap was measurement damage — c=4 contention plus five trials silently deleted from the denominator by a retry policy that couldn't tell a setup-phase `apt-get` failure from the agent getting the answer wrong. The other half was never real. The release gate says nothing is wrong with 0.9.11.

Two things left on the table, both your call:
- `mailman` still sits unscored in the 0.9.7 leg (86 of 89), which is the conservative direction, so I left it.
- The retry-classifier bug is unfixed. I haven't touched the script.

The brief at the artifact URL still carries last night's pre-re-run numbers. Want me to update it with the final ones?

**On the reasoning-effort point.** It's real — the dialect matrix in `client.rs` is genuinely ~40 arms of bespoke JSON shapes and OpenRouter is the one that passes through. But as an interview thesis it's weak, because "the aggregator normalizes things across providers" is just describing what an aggregator is *for*. Telling OpenRouter that their normalization layer is useful is telling them their product works. It's fine as a supporting detail; I over-ranked it by putting it at the top of the "what helped" list.

**On the auth thing.** Let me be accurate about what it actually is, because "outdated docs" isn't quite it: `/api/v1/models` is a public catalog endpoint, so it returns 200 whatever bearer you send — including garbage. If you reach for it as a key-validation probe (which is the obvious thing to do, and what I did), your login flow silently accepts bad keys. `/api/v1/auth/key` is the endpoint that actually answers "is this key real." That's a true behavior, not a docs error. But it's a papercut. Bringing it to a research interview is bringing a support ticket.

So: two of the things I put in front are filler. Here's my honest tiering of the material.

**Actually strong — thesis material, lead with these:**

- **Cost-optimal per-request routing is not cost-optimal per-trajectory.** `sort: "cost"` reshuffles the endpoint mid-trajectory, converts expected cache reads into fresh input at 5–10× the rate, and on a cost-plus bill the customer's total goes *up* while the operator's take goes down. This is non-obvious, specific to routers, and an open problem at their scale.
- **Agent workloads are a cache-read business.** 95.2M of 96.2M input tokens were cache reads in the leg I instrumented — 98.9%. Per-token headline price is a weak predictor of what agentic traffic actually costs. That reframes what a router should be optimizing.
- **Thirty endpoints, one slug, and price encodes neither quantization nor context.** The floor was fp4 at 262K; the *most expensive* endpoint was also fp4 with a truncated window. Measured from their own `/endpoints` feed.
- **The null results.** Two paired comparisons at p = 1.00, plus the power calculation showing an 89-task single-attempt suite needs ~4× the volume to resolve the differences people argue about. That's the research-scientist signal.

**Proof-of-contact — use only if asked "did you really build on this?":** revision pinning and the undated-slug trap, the fail-closed model-identity check, provider pinning flags, `input_cache_write`, `top_provider.context_length`, the aggregator concurrency profile.

content.text:
Exactly that. And you already used their hook for it without framing it that way — the worker sends `session_id` on OpenRouter routes only, derived from a hash of customer + product + trajectory, with any client-supplied value stripped first so a caller can't forge someone else's affinity key.

Here's the arithmetic that makes it concrete. Two real fp8 endpoints from your own `/endpoints` pull:

```
DeepInfra   fresh $0.080/M   cache read $0.016/M
StreamLake  fresh $0.067/M   cache read $0.013/M      (16% cheaper fresh)

Turn with a 200K accumulated prefix + 5K new content:

  stay on DeepInfra ......  200K cached + 5K fresh   = $0.0036
  switch to StreamLake ...  205K ALL fresh (cold)    = $0.0137   <- 3.8x
  steady on StreamLake ...  200K cached + 5K fresh   = $0.0029

  switch penalty ......... $0.0101
  saving per later turn .. $0.0007
  break-even ............. ~14 more turns
```

So to chase a 16% cheaper endpoint you need confidence the trajectory has **fourteen more turns left**. A per-request cost sort has no idea. It sees $0.067 < $0.080 and moves — and quadruples that turn's bill.

And the penalty *grows monotonically through the trajectory*, because the prefix does. Switching at turn 3 is nearly free; at turn 40 it's brutal. That structure is exploitable: you can be promiscuous early and sticky late, which is a real policy, not a heuristic.

**What the research problem decomposes into:**

1. **Cache state as routing input.** You can't decide without knowing which endpoints currently hold a warm prefix for this trajectory. That's per-endpoint, with unpublished TTLs and eviction behavior. Some endpoints don't report cache tokens at all — Codewhale pins `cache_telemetry_supported = false` on the OpenRouter DeepSeek route. You cannot manage what you cannot observe, and that's a first-order gap.

2. **Horizon prediction.** The break-even depends on turns remaining, and agent trajectories are viciously heavy-tailed — Microsoft's Orchard set has median 19K tokens, P95 39K, max 101K; the SWE-bench study reports up to 30× variance on the *same task* across runs. Predicting remaining horizon from the first few turns is its own paper.

3. **Warmth decays.** A cached prefix isn't binary. DeepSeek's is "hours to days, best effort." So the right object is P(still warm | endpoint, elapsed), and stickiness has a half-life.

4. **Formally it's a bandit with state-dependent switching costs.** Standard formulations assume a fixed switching penalty; here it scales with accumulated prefix. That's the interesting variant.

5. **And this is the part you're circling — the tension with load balancing.** If every trajectory sticks to its locally-cheapest endpoint, load concentrates and you lose the capacity and latency benefits of having a pool. But every rebalancing move destroys cache locality. So fleet-level balancing and per-trajectory locality are in direct conflict, and the currency to trade them in is dollars, which is computable. It's the same shape as CPU cache affinity in an OS scheduler or session affinity in a load balancer — except here the migration cost has an explicit price and you can measure whether you got it right.

**Why it's their problem specifically:** OpenRouter sees cache-hit outcomes across every endpoint and every app. Nobody else can measure realized cache-hit rate per endpoint, how fast it decays, or how it varies by upstream. The routing decision and the measurement apparatus are in the same place, which is rare.

**And the honest hard parts,** which you should volunteer rather than have them raised at you: they can't see prefix contents for privacy reasons, so affinity has to key on something pseudonymous; endpoints that don't report cache tokens are invisible to the whole scheme; and a trajectory-sticky router is a router that can't drain an unhealthy endpoint quickly, so health and locality fight too.

That's a real research agenda, it's specific to what OpenRouter is, and you arrived at it by hitting the problem in production rather than by reading about it. That should be the spine of the brief — want me to restructure it around this and demote the rest to an appendix?
